name: Ivan Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Tell me about a typical shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am a senior lineworker at an electricity company, usually leading the crew from the first truck check through the last repair note. I have a two-year technical diploma and a habit of taking a fault sketch home to see whether a better method exists. I use AI tools every day to sort those notes, but we still have to test a power line before touching it. The pay is lower than I think a lead should earn, and the mortgage and two children have left us almost no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that modest AI is already useful for sorting my sketches, and that is about as far as the change goes. The crew still brings the street back when a line breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like the tools more than I like our budget. We have less than one month of expenses put aside, and the few nearby lineworker posts would not be an easy escape if our company cut hours for ordinary reasons. AI can sort my fault sketches, but it cannot put a weekend lineworker wage in our empty emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the lead rota and keep checking every AI summary against the fault sheet. Starting this month, I would take one paid Saturday callout each month when offered and put thirty from it into a new emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested in the software, anxious about money. A quiet AI future leaves the same thin buffer under our family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What have you caught in an AI summary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It once called a cracked insulator a loose connector in a sketch summary. I corrected the work note before it reached the next shift, then showed the apprentice what the photograph actually showed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no Saturday callout that month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the thirty does not get saved that month; I will not pretend the cash appeared. My partner and I would keep the mortgage and school costs ahead of new purchases.

say: **Small** AI tools help me sort fault sketches while crews still repair power lines.
I would **keep** field checks before any AI summary reaches the next shift.
think: I **trust** useful software but worry about lower pay and savings below one month.
**Few** nearby lineworker posts limit the household’s fallback if ordinary hours shrink.
do: **Keep** leading shifts and check AI summaries against fault sheets.
**Save** thirty from each paid Saturday callout when offered.
feel: **Curious** about tools but anxious about existing household finances.
S0.quote: AI can sort my fault sketches, but it cannot put a weekend lineworker wage in our empty emergency account.
fieldNote: His **daily** AI use is established, but he catches errors by looking at real fault records.
**New** saving depends on an actual paid callout, which may not be offered every month.

steps.text: Keep lead shifts and check AI summaries against fault sheets
Save thirty from each paid Saturday callout if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say stronger AI may improve buying and dispatch, and I would volunteer to test its parts suggestions on actual repairs. The company should pay field workers for the testing instead of expecting a free second job after shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first cuts may land in the office, but a bad parts list can take an entire crew off a line for hours. I could become useful as a field tester, yet there is no room in our budget for unpaid trial work. A clever parts list is worth nothing when a line crew has to drive back for the missing insulator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep a log of suggested parts and the parts we actually use on each fault. In the first year of the new system I would show that log to the depot manager and ask for a paid tester shift; if the company offers it at my current rate, I would take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our thin savings, with some appetite to try the tool. I would be much less cheerful if management gave me extra checking without extra paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful log entry contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work order, suggested part, actual part and the time lost fetching a missing item. I want the depot manager to see whether the tool saves time on ordinary faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a tester title with no extra pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I already lead a crew on a low rate, and a new badge does not cover the mortgage. I would test during a normal paid shift only.

say: I would **test** AI parts suggestions against real line repairs.
**Field** testing should be paid work, with the crew able to correct wrong lists.
think: **Office** roles may change first, while bad purchasing AI could waste crew hours.
A **paid** tester duty might help, but unpaid work worsens our thin household budget.
do: **Log** suggested parts, actual parts and lost time on each fault.
**Ask** depot manager for paid tester shift after showing the log.
**Take** tester shift only if the company pays at least my current rate.
feel: **Anxious** about unpaid extra work but willing to test a useful system.
S1.quote: A clever parts list is worth nothing when a line crew has to drive back for the missing insulator.
fieldNote: He **sees** the first opportunity in field testing a thinking tool, rather than changing trade.
His **lower** pay makes paid time a firm condition, despite strong technical curiosity.

steps.text: Test AI parts suggestions against actual repair records
Take paid field tester shift if rate meets current wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew that full thinking AI by 2028 could write the plan, but robots able to work a line arrive around 2031. I would ask for a paid place testing robot isolation before a machine is allowed on a customer’s street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am keen to learn, but the clock scares me because our savings will not cover one full month without wages. A machine that takes the paid emergency callouts could make our mortgage late long before a new job appears nearby. I want to test the line robot, but our mortgage cannot live on curiosity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cut the family’s paid sports package this week and show the children why. Before 2028 I would apply for a paid robot test shift, and in the first year after thinking AI arrives I would ask my brother to cover school pickup on trial days if the company actually pays me for those shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and alert. I want a place on the test crew, but I will not put the family behind on the house payment to get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children about the sports package?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say we are keeping their school clubs but dropping a television package until work is clearer. I would not tell them a robot has taken my job when no such thing has happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask your brother for school pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother already lives near the school and has offered occasional pickup. I would ask only for paid trial shifts that clash with my partner’s work, not assume he is free every day.

say: I would **seek** paid robot isolation testing before capable machines work on streets around 2031.
The **crew** should test what thinking AI proposes before any robot follows it.
think: **Thin** savings and scarce nearby posts make lost emergency callouts dangerous for the mortgage.
**Curiosity** does not let me take an unpaid robot trial.
do: **Cancel** paid sports package while protecting children’s school clubs.
**Apply** for a paid robot test shift before 2028.
**Ask** my brother for school pickup on paid trial days that clash with partner’s work.
feel: **Anxious** about speed and pay, despite wanting to test the machines.
S2.quote: I want to test the line robot, but our mortgage cannot live on curiosity.
fieldNote: He **makes** a family cut now without telling children a job loss is certain.
**Family** pickup is conditional on a paid test shift and a genuine scheduling clash.

steps.text: Cancel family sports television package this week
Apply for paid company robot test shift before 2028
Ask brother for school pickup on conflicting paid trial days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that the extra years to thinking AI in 2031 and capable robots in 2034 give time to build a real field testing job. I would rather be paid to find a machine’s mistakes than watch a sales demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My diploma and lead experience might count for a test technician post, and I already use AI every day. Still, there are few such vacancies near us, and I cannot leave a low wage for no wage while a course runs. A robot test certificate is useful to my family only when the line company pays for the course and posts the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request the company’s test technician job description, salary and course funding. If it posts a local role covering our mortgage and funds the technical course on paid time, I would enroll before 2031 and apply when the role opens; otherwise I would stay on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our thin savings, but the long runway lets me check real terms. I am willing to move first on tools, not first into an unpaid hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course need to teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want fault simulation, robot stop controls and how to compare a machine’s plan with a live site. A glossy introduction would not qualify me to sign a test report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a distant technician vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without a written offer and a family discussion about moving the children. Few local openings are frustrating, but I cannot uproot them for a possibility.

say: The **longer** runway could support a paid field test technician route before robots arrive around 2034.
I would **check** machine mistakes on real sites, not just demonstrations.
think: My **technical** diploma and daily AI use could help if a funded local post exists.
**Unpaid** training or a distant speculative vacancy would expose our mortgage.
do: **Request** local technician job description, salary and funded course terms.
**Enroll** before 2031 if course is paid and suitable local role is posted.
**Apply** for posted local technician role if salary covers the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** but able to inspect actual job and training terms over time.
S3.quote: A robot test certificate is useful to my family only when the line company pays for the course and posts the job.
fieldNote: His **technical** confidence meets a hard household limit: paid study and a genuine local vacancy.
He **declines** to treat a distant vacancy as an automatic family move.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if technical course is paid and suitable local role posted
Apply for posted local test technician role if salary covers mortgage
Keep line shifts if funded course or suitable role is absent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade before full thinking AI and three more years before capable robots is enough time to teach apprentices both the old line craft and the new checks. I would build a short fault diagram lesson that starts with the pole, not the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three, I might prefer paid teaching over night callouts, but I cannot count on the mortgage being gone. If a few apprentices pay for extra diagram practice now, that would build a small second income without gambling our last savings on equipment. A power line diagram lesson costs me paper; a bad career gamble costs my children their home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would offer two Saturday fault diagram sessions at the library this year for a modest fee, using the sketches I already own. If apprentices book and pay, I would run them while keeping my electricity company shifts; later I would apply for a paid company trainer role only if its salary covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about next month’s bills, but I like being able to start small. The decade gives me room to see whether teaching suits me before any robot takes a climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge and spend to start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask ten per apprentice for a two-hour session and use printed copies of my own diagrams. If nobody books, I would cancel the session rather than pay for a room or new equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What permission would you need from your employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the company’s outside-work rules before taking any payment and keep customer details out of the lessons. If the rules bar it, I would drop the side sessions and keep my lead shifts.

say: I would **teach** apprentices field fault diagrams before capable robots reach line work around 2039.
**Paid** lessons must respect company rules and use no customer details.
think: A **small** teaching income could help the thin savings cushion without buying equipment.
**Any** later company trainer role still needs enough pay for the mortgage.
do: **Check** outside-work rules before charging for apprentice lessons.
**Run** two paid Saturday diagram sessions if permitted and apprentices book.
**Apply** for company trainer role later only if posted salary covers mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills, though encouraged by a small paid experiment.
S4.quote: A power line diagram lesson costs me paper; a bad career gamble costs my children their home.
fieldNote: His **entrepreneurial** side stays small because the household cannot risk capital or unpaid time.
**Paid** sessions require company permission and actual apprentice bookings, while a trainer job needs sufficient salary.

steps.text: Run two paid Saturday diagram sessions if permitted and apprentices book
Apply for posted company trainer role if salary covers mortgage
Keep electricity company lead shifts while testing paid lessons

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robot trials and lost callouts could collide with our thin savings by around 2031. Paid test shifts, clear fault responsibility and a training post with an actual wage would help. My children cannot eat a promise that the power line company will find me something later.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the company will let workers test a new tool on paid time before calling it safe. I am ready to learn, but I will not use the children’s mortgage money to finance the company’s experiment. The crew’s field knowledge has a price.

headlineQuote: My children cannot eat a promise that the power line company will find me something later.
portrait: **Ivan** is a forty-three-year-old electricity company lineworker who leads repairs, has a technical diploma and uses AI tools daily for fault notes.
His **lower-than-usual** pay, mortgage and two school-age children leave less than one month of savings despite senior standing.
He **volunteers** to test parts lists and line robots, but paid time and a real local post are firm conditions.
With a **decade**, he tries small paid diagram lessons for apprentices while preserving shifts and checking employer permission.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could let lost callouts and robot trials reach his thin household cushion before wages recover.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** test shifts, clear fault responsibility and a funded training route into an actual local job would help.
